abstract.text:
We analyze the effect of rising Chinese import competition between
1990 and 2007 on US local labor markets, exploiting ­cross-market
variation in import exposure stemming from initial differences in
industry specialization and instrumenting for US imports using
changes in Chinese imports by other high-income countries. Rising
imports cause higher unemployment, lower labor force participation,
and reduced wages in local labor markets that house i­mportcompeting manufacturing industries. In our main specification,
import competition explains one-quarter of the contemporaneous
aggregate decline in US manufacturing employment. Transfer
benefits payments for unemployment, disability, retirement, and
healthcare also rise sharply in more trade-exposed labor markets.
(JEL E24, F14, F16, J23, J31, L60, O47, R12, R23)

thesis.text: Rising Chinese import competition caused higher unemployment, lower labor-force participation, reduced wages, and increased transfer-benefit reliance in more exposed US local labor markets.

citations.context: The past two decades have seen a fruitful debate on the impact of international trade on US labor markets (Feenstra 2010).

While in the 1980s, trade in the form of foreign outsourcing was associated with modest increases in the wage premium for skilled manufacturing labor (Feenstra and Hanson 1999), the evidence suggests that other shocks, including skill biased technical change, played a more important role in the evolution of the US wage structure in that decade (Katz and Autor 1999).
citations.reference_key: Feenstra and Hanson 1999; Katz and Autor 1999

citations.context: Beginning in the 1990s, the literature developed rapidly as economists sought to understand the forces behind rising US wage inequality.
One factor limiting trade’s impact on US labor is that historically, imports from low-wage countries have been small (Krugman 2000).

Though freer trade with countries at any income level may affect wages and employment, trade theory identifies low-wage countries as a likely source of disruption to high-wage labor markets (Krugman 2008).

Commuting zones (CZs), which encompass all metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas in the United States, are logical geographic units for defining local labor markets (Tolbert and Sizer 1996; Autor and Dorn 2013).
citations.reference_key: Tolbert and Sizer 1996; Autor and Dorn 2013

citations.context: In light of the internal and global external factors driving China’s exports, we instrument for the growth in US imports from China using Chinese import growth in other high-income markets. This approach requires that import demand shocks in high-income countries are not the primary cause of China’s export surge.

Our identification strategy is related to that used by Bloom, Draca, and Van Reenen (2011), who consider the relationship between imports from China and innovation in Europe. See also Auer and Fischer (2008).
citations.reference_key: Bloom, Draca, and Van Reenen 2011; Auer and Fischer 2008

citations.context: Our local labor market approach to analyzing the impacts of trade exposure follows important early work by Borjas and Ramey (1995), who also emphasize the role of trade imbalances in mapping trade shocks to labor-market outcomes, as well as more recent work by Chiquiar (2008), Topalova (2005, 2010), and Kovak (2013), who study the effects of trade liberalizations on wages, poverty, and migration in local and regional labor markets in Mexico, India, and Brazil, respectively.
citations.reference_key: Borjas and Ramey 1995; Chiquiar 2008; Topalova 2005, 2010; Kovak 2013

citations.context: The literature on regional adjustment to labor-market shocks suggests that mobility responses to labor demand shocks across US cities and states are slow and incomplete (Topel 1986; Blanchard and Katz 1992; Glaeser and Gyourko 2005).
citations.reference_key: Topel 1986; Blanchard and Katz 1992; Glaeser and Gyourko 2005

citations.context: Mobility is lowest for noncollege workers, who are overrepresented in manufacturing (Bound and Holzer 2000; Notowidigdo 2010).

The sluggish response of regional labor supply to import exposure may be related to the costly mobility of labor between sectors, as documented by Artuç, Chaudhuri, and McLaren (2010) in the United States and Dix-Carneiro (2011) in Brazil, also in the context of adjustment to trade shocks.

Theory suggests that trade with China yields aggregate gains for the US economy. Our study also highlights the distributional consequences of trade and the medium-run efficiency losses associated with adjustment to trade shocks.

sections.summary: Introduces the China trade shock, states the main empirical finding that import competition raised unemployment, cut participation and wages, and increased transfer receipts, and outlines the paper’s local-labor-market strategy.
sections.title: Introduction and headline results

source_span.end_text: B. Empirical Approach
source_span.start_text: I. Theoretical Motivation and Empirical Approach

sections.summary: Develops the monopolistic-competition trade model linking Chinese export-supply shocks to regional wages and employment, then defines the import-exposure measure and the other-high-income-country instrumental variable.
sections.title: Theory and empirical strategy

source_span.end_text: III. The Impact of Trade Shocks on Manufacturing Employment
source_span.start_text: II. Data Sources and Measurement

sections.summary: Describes UN Comtrade trade data, commuting zones, County Business Patterns industry employment, Census/ACS labor-market outcomes, and BEA/SSA transfer-payment data.
sections.title: Data and measurement

source_span.end_text: B. Benchmarking the Impact of China Trade Exposure On US Manufacturing
source_span.start_text: III. The Impact of Trade Shocks on Manufacturing Employment

sections.summary: Presents 2SLS estimates showing that rising Chinese import exposure significantly reduces manufacturing employment, with robustness to controls and benchmarking to aggregate US manufacturing decline.
sections.title: Manufacturing employment effects

source_span.end_text: IV. Beyond Manufacturing: Trade Shocks and Local Labor Markets
source_span.start_text: B. Benchmarking the Impact of China Trade Exposure On US Manufacturing

sections.summary: Benchmarks the supply-driven component of Chinese imports and compares China with other low-income, Mexico/CAFTA, and other-country imports.
sections.title: Benchmarking and non-China trade

source_span.end_text: B. Wage Effects
source_span.start_text: IV. Beyond Manufacturing: Trade Shocks and Local Labor Markets

sections.summary: Shows little population mobility in response to trade shocks, but large increases in unemployment and labor-force nonparticipation, with SSDI take-up accounting for part of the employment loss.
sections.title: Population, employment status, and SSDI

source_span.end_text: V. Public Transfer Payments and Household Incomes
source_span.start_text: B. Wage Effects

sections.summary: Finds significant negative effects of import exposure on average weekly earnings, with nonmanufacturing wages falling while manufacturing wages do not.
sections.title: Wage effects

source_span.end_text: VI. Exports and the Factor Content of Trade
source_span.start_text: V. Public Transfer Payments and Household Incomes

sections.summary: Shows that import exposure raises transfer payments, especially disability and medical benefits, and reduces household wage and salary income.
sections.title: Public transfers and household income

source_span.end_text: VII. Losses in Efficiency from Use of Public Benefits and Involuntary Labor Force Nonparticipation
source_span.start_text: VI. Exports and the Factor Content of Trade

sections.summary: Tests alternative trade-exposure measures: international exposure, intermediate inputs, net imports, gravity residuals, and factor content of trade.
sections.title: Alternative trade exposure measures

source_span.end_text: VIII. Conclusion
source_span.start_text: VII. Losses in Efficiency from Use of Public Benefits and Involuntary Labor Force Nonparticipation

sections.summary: Quantifies deadweight losses from transfer take-up and involuntary nonparticipation, then concludes that China trade had distributional and medium-run efficiency consequences for exposed US labor markets.
sections.title: Efficiency losses and conclusion

abstract.text:
We analyze the effect of rising Chinese import competition between
1990 and 2007 on US local labor markets, exploiting ­cross-market
variation in import exposure stemming from initial differences in
industry specialization and instrumenting for US imports using
changes in Chinese imports by other high-income countries. Rising
imports cause higher unemployment, lower labor force participation,
and reduced wages in local labor markets that house i­mportcompeting manufacturing industries. In our main specification,
import competition explains one-quarter of the contemporaneous
aggregate decline in US manufacturing employment. Transfer
benefits payments for unemployment, disability, retirement, and
healthcare also rise sharply in more trade-exposed labor markets.
(JEL E24, F14, F16, J23, J31, L60, O47, R12, R23)

thesis.text: Rising Chinese import competition caused higher unemployment, lower labor-force participation, reduced wages, and increased transfer-benefit reliance in more exposed US local labor markets.

citations.context: The past two decades have seen a fruitful debate on the impact of international trade on US labor markets (Feenstra 2010).

While in the 1980s, trade in the form of foreign outsourcing was associated with modest increases in the wage premium for skilled manufacturing labor (Feenstra and Hanson 1999), the evidence suggests that other shocks, including skill biased technical change, played a more important role in the evolution of the US wage structure in that decade (Katz and Autor
citations.reference_key: Feenstra and Hanson 1999; Katz and Autor 1999

citations.context: Beginning in the 1990s, the literature developed rapidly as economists sought to understand the forces behind rising US wage inequality.
One factor limiting trade’s impact on US labor is that historically, imports from low-wage countries have been small (Krugman 2000).

Though freer trade with countries at any income level may affect wages and employment, trade theory identifies low-wage countries as a likely source of disruption to high-wage labor markets (Krugman 2008).

Commuting zones (CZs), which encompass all metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas in the United States, are logical geographic units for defining local labor markets (Tolbert and Sizer 1996; Autor and Dorn 2013).
citations.reference_key: Tolbert and Sizer 1996; Autor and Dorn 2013

citations.context: In light of the internal and global external factors driving China’s exports, we instrument for the growth in US imports from China using Chinese import growth in other high-income markets.⁶ This approach requires that import demand shocks in high-income countries are not the primary cause of China’s export surge.

Our identification strategy is related to that used by Bloom, Draca, and Van Reenen (2011), who consider the relationship between imports from China and innovation in Europe. See also Auer and Fischer (2008).
